scenes.heading: Factors affecting photosynthesis and respiration
scenes.sub: Why greenhouses pump in extra CO₂
scenes.say: Why do some greenhouses pump in extra carbon dioxide? Photosynthesis and respiration are enzyme-controlled pathways, so their rates depend on conditions. In exams you'll often have to explain a rate graph, so let's learn how.

scenes.heading: Think of it like this
scenes.everyday: 100 sausages but only 30 slices of bread: you can only sell 30
scenes.science: The factor in shortest supply limits the rate
scenes.breaks: in a leaf, several factors interact, so the limiting factor can change gradually rather than at one sharp point.
scenes.say: At a sausage sizzle, if you have a hundred sausages but only thirty slices of bread, you can only sell thirty. Bread is the limiting factor. Buy more bread and sales rise, until sausages run out. A limiting factor is whatever is in shortest supply.
scenes.caption: At a sausage sizzle, if you have 100 sausages but only 30 slices of bread, you can only sell 30. Bread is the limiting factor. Buy more bread and sales rise, until sausages run out. A limiting factor is whatever is in shortest supply.

scenes.heading: Photosynthesis factors
points: More light: more ATP and NADPH, until a plateau
More CO₂: Rubisco works faster, until a plateau
High O₂: more photorespiration, lower rate
Water shortage closes stomata, so less CO₂
scenes.say: More light means more ATP and NADPH for the Calvin cycle, until the rate plateaus. More carbon dioxide fills Rubisco's active sites more often. High oxygen increases photorespiration and lowers the rate. And thirsty plants shut the windows: water shortage closes stomata, so carbon dioxide can't get in.

scenes.heading: Respiration factors
points: Low O₂: more fermentation, less ATP
More glucose: faster, until a plateau
scenes.say: For respiration, oxygen is the final electron acceptor, so more oxygen speeds it up until it's no longer limiting. Low oxygen means more fermentation and far less ATP. More glucose raises the rate until enzymes are saturated.

scenes.heading: Temperature (both)
scenes.say: Temperature affects both pathways like any enzyme. Warmer molecules collide more often, so the rate rises to an optimum. Above that, enzymes denature and the rate drops fast. Hot breaks, cold slows.

scenes.heading: Worked example
scenes.question: Rate vs light: at 0.04% CO₂ it plateaus at 10 units; at 0.4% CO₂ it plateaus at 25 units. Explain.
lines: Low light: lines overlap, light limiting
scenes.say: At low light, both lines overlap, so light is limiting. The lower curve flattens at ten units, so carbon dioxide is now limiting. Adding more raises the plateau to twenty-five, which proves it. Then something else, like temperature, takes over.
scenes.caption: At low light, both lines overlap, so light is limiting. The lower curve flattens at 10 units, so CO₂ is now limiting. Adding more raises the plateau to 25, which proves it. Then something else, like temperature, takes over.

scenes.heading: Reading a rate graph

left.title: Rising part
points: Increase it and the rate rises

scenes.say: Here's the trick: rising means the x-axis factor is limiting. Flat means something else is. For every section, describe with data, explain using the pathway, and name the limiting factor.

Quick recap. The limiting factor is the one in shortest supply. A plateau means another factor has taken over. Light and carbon dioxide boost photosynthesis, oxygen and glucose boost respiration, and too much heat denatures enzymes. Now try the practice questions!
